title: Webpack Optimisation and Internals
body: [https://ke.qq.com/webcourse/1647350/103691469#taid=12145403010556662&vid=387702293148710449](https://ke.qq.com/webcourse/1647350/103691469#taid=12145403010556662&vid=387702293148710449) Video playback engines are all WebAssembly now. Webpack's weak spot is JavaScript. JavaScript runs in a JIT, and it needs an engine to run at all. That is the environment Webpack lives in, and its speed is capped by the JS engine. Badly written JavaScript makes Webpack slow. But however much you optimise, you have already handed the work to a black box. **OSS** — cloud object storage. **Jump box (bastion host)** — sits between the internal network and the outside, controlling how external users or admins reach the inside. Its main job is to harden the internal network. It also works as a central node for managing and monitoring internal servers and devices. # Optimising Webpack 4 ## I/O ### Upgrade Webpack itself Webpack is slow mostly because I/O is slow. Webpack does a lot of I/O — constant input and output. Frequent I/O is what makes it slow, so keep the entry small and stop the I/O growing. (This matters for the dev server's HMR, for persistent caching, and for the packing entry that reads a pile of files out of a directory.) There are only two reasons for a blank page: **the JavaScript threw, or the request never came back.** If the request never came back you get a spinner. `eval` emits code fast but runs slowly in the browser. What `eval` gives you: 1. dynamic execution; 2. its own scope — each module goes into an `eval` function, so modules stay isolated from one another. What it costs: a string has to be turned into code before it runs, which is slow, and it is not safe. Webpack's dev-mode bundle uses `eval` to speed up bundling and execution and to cut both code size and transfer time. ### Many entries? Build across machines. scripty + **Cluster builds** Set up passwordless SSH between your machine and three machines in the office. When the app is ready to build, send commands to all three, let them build in turn, and `scp` the results back. One machine's workload is now spread across four. ### Tree shaking You have to set `optimization.usedExports` before unused code is actually removed from the output. ## Tooling **The official plugin list lives here → https://webpack.js.org/awesome-webpack/** ### speed-measure-webpack-plugin - **Measures how long each step takes.** Watch the third-party packages in particular. + friendly-errors-webpack-plugin ### Replace pages of build output with one line progress-bar-webpack-plugin gives you a progress bar. ### Show the current stage in the iTerm2 title bar `set-iterm2-badge` and `node-bash-title`, to see which steps are slow. ### prepack-webpack-plugin **Webpack 5 absorbed Prepack — a static JavaScript evaluator. Pure functions get evaluated away at build time.** ### Why do production builds take so long? **Production code takes longer to run and is more complex, and minification costs time.** **For production, combine a hosted SDK with a production build to get the final result.** (So do not assume that a performance problem in development means one in production.) ### Too much currying leaks memory — currying is closures underneath. ## Caching **Caching trades space for time, and it does waste space. These days the cache sits in memory.** ### cache-loader **It caches everything. Anything that has not changed is not recompiled, which shortens babel-loader's work too.** **Turning it on in Webpack 4 makes an immediate difference. Webpack 5 has it built in.** ### hard-source-webpack-plugin **Caches the whole project** — loaders, plugins, compilation. It gets faster the more you use it, and it is said to beat cache-loader. It no longer works on Webpack 5. Webpack's ecosystem beats Vite's. It absorbs other tools' features. ## Mechanics ### Multithreading: terser-webpack-plugin (minification can go parallel) Be careful with threads in JavaScript — turning them on can make the build *slower*. JS threads are expensive, and switching between them costs a lot. **happypack** — the Webpack 4 plugin for parallel builds. **Webpack 5 replaced it with thread-loader.** + **The compile pipeline, in miniature** ```javascript function compile(sourceCode) { const tokens = tokenize(sourceCode); const ast = parse(tokens); const optimizedAst = optimize(ast); const targetCode = generate(optimizedAst); return targetCode; } ``` ### Getting out of JavaScript entirely: esbuild-loader, swc-loader **Stop running the compilation through the JIT and do it in a lower-level language.** Babel is written in JavaScript, so it has to go through the JIT and is necessarily slow. Go and Rust are far faster. **esbuild is written in Go and has its own tree shaking, which conflicts with Webpack 5's Prepack — use esbuild and you lose Prepack. Your build then uses esbuild's shaking, which is the older mechanism.** **swc is written in Rust and replaces Babel. With it, you get roughly the same speed as babel-loader with hard-source-webpack-plugin enabled.** swc-loader in place of Babel. # Optimising Webpack 5 ### Webpack 5 builds in parallel out of the box. ### Set `parallel: true`. The threading is built on the Worker Pool API. ### thread-loader (**Even though Webpack 5 has parallel builds built in, thread-loader is still worth using.** It moves expensive tasks onto worker threads — **not** web workers — for parallel processing, which speeds the build up further. It can compile and bundle JavaScript, CSS, Less, Sass and more across several worker threads.) **thread-loader's threading** is implemented with **Node's `child_process` module.** ### Persistent caching and incremental builds — why HMR is fast in dev **`cache.type = filesystem`** — persistent cache **`cache.provided = true`** — incremental builds **Webpack 5's output can still contain plenty of ES6 — `let`, `const`, and so on. Babel only handles your project's code, not Webpack's own runtime.** ### Prepack **Prepack is about making the code run faster and read more clearly.** **Let Webpack 5's tree shaking remove the unused code first, then let Prepack optimise and simplify what is left.** ### Static assets **All the loaders you needed for CSS and images are gone; you just declare the file as an asset.** **If you use Less or Sass you still need loaders.** **Fonts, images, SVG — all of it handled by `type: 'asset'`.** **`cache.type` takes two values:** **`memory` for an in-memory cache, `filesystem` for a persistent one.** # How Webpack works inside ## Implementing CommonJS **A Webpack 4 bundle is an IIFE closure that implements CommonJS: every module goes into one object under a key, and you pull out whichever you need.** `eval` is fast in development, but development performance numbers differ from a production build. Do not build your production code with your development setup — you will hit strange problems. All the dev environment has to prove is that the feature works. **Read up on source maps, and on why `eval` is fast in development.** Read up on the trade-offs between ESM and CommonJS. In the finished bundle, `__webpack_require__` loads each module by `moduleId`. Read up on magic comments. ## The Webpack lifecycle The whole build is built on `Compiler`. **Multi-core compilation. It pays off on a large project.** **When people say Webpack is slow, they mean the loaders.** **One loader finishes and hands off to the next, and that handoff is slow.** I did not follow this part: after a loader walks the AST and produces a string, does the next loader parse it back into an AST? ## Parcel + Why Parcel is fast: one AST, and every loader runs against it end to end. It converts every file into a single AST, merges all the loaders internally into one, and has them all operate on that same AST. That removes the string I/O between loaders and the repeated work. + Where Parcel fits + How Babel runs, end to end The ES6 AST becomes an ES5 AST, and code is generated from that. When a plugin runs depends on when its hooks are registered. Tapable is what wires Webpack's files together. Is Vue's LRU tied to keep-alive? Does `with` really stop the whole current scope from being collected? Its template would then live in memory permanently. ## Minifying the bundle
